item.title: 'Trump has cost us': MAGA loyalists question his future after midterm losses
item.description:
By Ned Parker, John Shiffman, Mike Spector, Peter Eisler and Linda So

DALLAS, Nov 8 (Reuters) - As Republicans faced a nationwide drubbing in Tuesday’s midterm elections, supporters streamed out of a Dallas ballroom where they’d hoped to toast a win for US Senate candidate Ken Paxton, a favorite of President Donald Trump.

In the hotel bar, Michael Little, a 59-year-old businessman and three-time Trump voter, stared at the president’s image on a television screen. “People are pissed off at Trump. Trump has cost us,” he said, capturing a sentiment rippling through the president’s Make America Great Again movement after the Republican Party’s worst electoral defeat in decades.

Across the coalition, some supporters who once viewed Trump as MAGA’s greatest asset are beginning to question whether he’s become its biggest liability.

The midterm losses amounted to more than a repudiation of Trump. They were a referendum on the political and cultural movement he built. A defining ‌force in American politics that began as a campaign slogan during Trump’s 2016 presidential run now faces a potentially existential reckoning after voters disillusioned with soaring fuel prices, the Iran war and Washington corruption delivered Democrats decisive congressional majorities.

Trump’s first major response to the midterms came on Friday. Instead of changing course, he doubled down on the movement’s core. He promoted Stephen Miller, the main architect of the administration’s hardline immigration crackdown, to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Wiles was seen ‌as a stabilizing force inside an often chaotic White House.

The move was celebrated by some of MAGA’s most ardent influencers, who saw it as a return to the anti-immigration agenda at the movement’s roots. “Exactly the energy we need,” right-wing influencer Benny Johnson posted on X to his 4.1 million followers. “Solid move. It’s Miller Time.”

The White House did not directly answer Reuters' questions about why Republicans lost, the defeat of candidates who embraced Trump's false 2020 election claims, or where MAGA goes from here. Instead, it pointed to Trump's remarks on Wednesday, when he said, "If I were on the ballot, we would have won." He also said it was "largely true" that the Iran war had ​cost Republicans because "it drove the gasoline up," but that he’d do it again.

For nearly a decade, MAGA has reshaped the Republican Party and transformed national debates on issues such as trade, immigration, race and gender. The movement installed loyalists throughout federal agencies, cracked down on immigration and pressured corporations and public institutions to retreat from diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. MAGA survived the fallout from the January 6, 2021, attack on the US Capitol and propelled Trump back to the White House. In Trump’s second term, MAGA was no longer a faction of the Republican Party; it was the party.

Now, the Democrats’ sweeping victory has forced the movement to grapple with an unexpected question: Is MAGA over?

Reuters interviews with more than a dozen MAGA activists, influencers, party strategists, Christian nationalist leaders and researchers who track right-wing politics, along with a review of MAGA supporters' posts and podcasts since Tuesday, show a movement turning its anger on itself.

The stolen-election claims that have driven MAGA since Democrat Joe Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election have mostly gone quiet. Instead, supporters are blaming Republican leaders and Trump's advisers, and in some cases the president himself, for broken promises on living costs, the Iran war and the government’s decision to redact or withhold major portions of its investigative files on late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

MAGA’s factions also disagree about what comes next. Some want a return to populist and nationalist basics. Some want a movement less tied to one man. And a vocal minority say MAGA is already dead.

“We have to rebuild,” Steve Bannon, a prominent MAGA proponent, podcaster and former Trump White House adviser, told Reuters. He urged the party to double down on an aggressive populist and nationalist agenda and praised Trump for elevating Miller. “Miller's appointment ‌as chief of staff underpins my point,” he said. “There is no more hardcore MAGA proponent than Stephen.”

As pro-Trump internet forums digested the election results, a notable slice of self-described MAGA loyalists – ⁠more than 20% – raised doubts about the movement’s leadership and direction, according to an analysis of social media traffic done for Reuters by PeakMetrics, a data intelligence firm. About half of that cohort remained supportive of the MAGA movement but no longer backed Trump as its leader. The other half remained loyal to, though critical of, the president himself.

The analysis was based on 12,850 posts sampled from a universe of 4.6 million Trump-related comments on X and Reddit from 9 p.m. on Election Day to 8 p.m. the next evening. It found broad concern among MAGA supporters as the results became clear. Of the posts that assigned blame for the rout, nearly a third said concerns about the Iran war and Israel’s influence over US policy had overshadowed Trump’s message. A quarter said Republicans not fully committed to the MAGA agenda had undermined ⁠the movement.

The results left Trump facing large Democratic majorities in both chambers of Congress. Democrats could hold as many as 56 of the Senate's 100 seats, more than enough to block his judicial nominees. They will also hold governorships in all seven battleground states Trump won in 2024, and they swept every statewide race in Texas, which last backed a Democrat for president in 1976.

Some prominent Republicans, long wary of a MAGA base that punished dissent, have begun openly criticizing Trump.

Republican US Senator Ron Johnson of Wisconsin said on Saturday that corruption was present in “all branches of government,” including “I’m sad to say, within the Trump administration.” He cited Calley Means, a former White House adviser who told "The Joe Rogan Experience" podcast on Friday that Trump's top aides catered to special interests and blocked policies popular with Trump’s Make America Healthy Again movement. Voters "were expecting us to drain the swamp, but it seems like the swamp won," Johnson told Fox News.

Asked about Johnson's remarks and Means' accusations, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster did not address the corruption allegations, saying Trump had "made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again."

On Sunday, Republican US Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, who won reelection despite his party's losses, called Trump’s promotion of ​Miller a “bad mistake.” “You ​don’t promote those who were in charge,”  Stutzman told CNN. “He’s not liked out here in the Midwest by people. They don’t like his tone,” he said of Miller.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Miller had "been a key player” in delivering on Trump's agenda “since day one" and would "continue to deliver historic successes" as ​chief of staff. The White House also pointed to statements from 19 Republican lawmakers supporting Miller’s promotion.

‘MAGA IS STALE’

The midterm losses have muffled one of MAGA's loudest refrains: Since Tuesday, talk of election fraud ‌has virtually vanished among right-wing influencers.

“I have been banging the drum of rigged and stolen elections since 2020, but that is not why we lost the midterms,” Rogan O’Handley, a MAGA influencer who posts under the name DC_Draino, wrote on X to his 2.3 million followers. “We lost because we failed to fix the things voters sent us to do.” He didn’t respond to a request for comment.

After the 2020 election, Trump supporter Isabella DeLuca was among thousands who stormed the US Capitol on January 6, 2021. She was charged with five crimes, including theft of a table from inside the Capitol, and pleaded not guilty. Her case was dismissed after Trump returned to office and pardoned her.

This time, the 26-year-old conservative influencer directed her anger toward what she described as out-of-touch Republican leaders who failed to appeal to Gen Z voters on affordability, avoiding foreign wars and other key issues.

“Republicans were just lazy. They felt like that they were entitled to people's votes and that people would vote for them no matter what,” DeLuca told Reuters. “It goes to show you that you do have to earn people's votes, and that even in a super red state like Texas, you're not untouchable.”

The MAGA movement this year appeared "tired," she said.

That sentiment was echoed in online right-wing forums, said Jennifer Golbeck, a University of Maryland professor who has analyzed MAGA-related posts since 2016. She said engagement by Trump’s most loyal backers has steadily declined since January, including a 27% drop in posts and comments on Patriots.Win, a popular MAGA forum.

”The enthusiasm and the passion even among this hardest core group of supporters hasn't really been there," Golbeck said. "They are saying that ‘MAGA is stale.’ It’s not new and exciting like it once was.”

Fox News, a cable network that has long been a key platform for MAGA voices, saw a sharp decline in viewership ahead of the midterms, with its total daytime audience down 27% in October from a year earlier, according to Nielsen, the audience measurement firm. In a statement to Reuters, Fox said it drew more viewers than its cable-news rivals on election night. “FOX News has been the number one network in cable news for a quarter century,” the network said.

Some prominent right-wing influencers blamed the president’s advisers ‌or Republican lawmakers – but rarely Trump himself – for ignoring key voter concerns. In posts, online broadcasts and interviews with Reuters, many blamed dissatisfaction with the economy, though they differed on other reasons for Tuesday's results.

It wasn't just failure to address affordability that "crushed" Republicans, said Ben Shapiro, co-founder of the conservative ​site Daily Wire, on his online show on Wednesday. “If you’re talking about an electoral catastrophe – a wipeout like we saw last night – you need more ingredients. Here are the other ingredients: chaos and corruption.”

Laura Loomer, an influencer close to Trump, wrote on X: “America is over and the American Dream is dead.” Yet she told Reuters the ​losses did not signal the end of MAGA, arguing that anyone seeking the 2028 Republican presidential nomination would need Trump’s base.

“The Republican Party belongs to President Trump,” Loomer said. “The MAGA movement is still the majority of the GOP base, and whoever wants to run ​for president in 2028 on the GOP ticket, they would be unwise to be dismissive of President Trump.”

On Thursday, Loomer put her podcast on hiatus, saying she had been "running on empty for too long" and needed to focus on her personal life and upcoming wedding. She’ll return in January, she added.

BROKEN PROMISES

The midterms also tested the beliefs that have held MAGA together, and some of them are giving way.

The Democratic sweep dealt a significant setback ‌to the election denial movement, a central pillar of MAGA politics since Trump's 2020 defeat. Candidates who embraced his false claims of widespread voter fraud lost heavily, including several who had ​worked to overturn the 2020 result. Election deniers will hold at least 41 fewer congressional and statewide offices next year, and they have lost ​70% of the called races for statewide posts that oversee elections, according to States United Action, a nonprofit that tracks such candidates. Trump made no effort to contest the results and instead blamed Republicans for the defeat.

With few close races and no credible basis for a challenge, many prominent pro-Trump election skeptics dropped fraud allegations and urged supporters to keep organizing. A handful of allies still alleged, without evidence, that the vote was rigged. Mike Lindell, the MyPillow founder and promoter of false claims that machines flipped votes in 2020, said he was not concerned by Trump's pledge to accept the results. “That's his opinion. I've got a different opinion,” Lindell told Reuters. “I think it's all been stolen.”

But such claims stayed largely on the fringe, even among Republicans. Without contested races, the MAGA election denial movement risks losing the money, attention and momentum that sustained it. "Nobody's going to be putting money behind it," said Wendy Via, co-founder of the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism, a nonprofit that tracks ​hate speech and extremism.

Retired Lieutenant General Mike Flynn, who falsely claimed the 2020 election was stolen and is a popular figure in the Christian nationalist wing of the MAGA movement, accepted the defeat. He ‌called the results “a massacre” and criticized Trump and his administration for failing to deliver on pledges ranging from lowering costs to releasing the government’s investigative files on Epstein.

Responding to Vice President JD Vance’s assessment on X that the Iran war was “the reason we lost,” Flynn wrote: “the sheer number of broken promises is why the blue tsunami happened."

Flynn also criticized Christian voters for failing to show up. “As a Catholic and a Christian, I’m sorely embarrassed and disappointed,” he ​wrote.

Other prominent Christian nationalists were divided over whether MAGA can outlast Trump.

Douglas Wilson, a Christian nationalist pastor who was invited by US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to deliver a sermon at the Pentagon in February, told Reuters that MAGA “is not going anywhere” but must become less personality-driven and more focused on border control, tax cuts and avoiding foreign wars.

Joel Webbon, a far-right Christian nationalist pastor from Texas, was far less sanguine. “Trump lost this all by himself,” ​he said in a video on X, arguing that the president abandoned his base by embracing Israel, launching the war in Iran and failing to follow through on releasing the Epstein files and mass deportations.

“MAGA is dead,” Webbon wrote in an accompanying post.  “Forever.”

(Editing by Jason Szep)

This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-cost-us-midterm-losses-110625474.html

item.title: 杀人犯也要分左右？
item.description:
来源: 
来稿

波兰克拉科夫发生大规模枪击案，六人死亡，十多人受伤，枪手还涉嫌杀害自己的父母和姐姐。如此惨案，理应首先关注死者、伤者，以及凶手为何行凶。不料新闻报道很快出现了另一个重点：枪手有极右翼思想。

波兰内政部长宣布，种种迹象显示，凶手沉迷于极右翼意识形态。一些媒体随即在报道中突出这一说法。读者还没弄清楚凶手为什么杀人，倒先知道了他在政治光谱上的位置。

这年头，杀人也要先分左右，仿佛凶手拿的是左手枪还是右手枪，比枪口对准谁更有新闻价值。

问题是，左派一定杀人吗？右派一定屠杀吗？全世界有多少左派、右派，一辈子连鸡都没有杀过。一个人犯下滔天罪行，为什么急着替他寻找政治亲戚？

如果凶手留下宣言，宣布为实现某种政治目标而杀人，政治思想当然是重大新闻。但如果只是官员声称他持有某种观点，而尚未公开足以证明作案动机的证据，媒体凭什么把政治标签摆在显眼位置？

更有意思的是，波兰网络上随后流传出疑似凶手的社交媒体旧帖。有的照片涉及彩虹旗，有的拿共产主义开玩笑，还有参加妇女抗议活动的说法。波兰当地媒体也报道了与官方判断不同的调查线索。

这些材料尚未全部得到独立核实，更不能凭几张照片就断定凶手是左派。但它们至少提出一个问题：内政部长究竟掌握了什么证据？

答案并不复杂：谁主张，谁举证。

政府官员的话当然可以报道，却不是什么金科玉律。官员有政治立场，也可能掌握不完整的信息。尤其在政治斗争激烈的国家，一句官方定性更不应该代替事实调查。

一些媒体或许会辩解，标题已经写明“当局称”，并没有直接把官员说法当成事实。然而，新闻报道不仅要考虑每句话是否有出处，还要考虑为什么选择突出这句话。

一家餐馆发生食物中毒，记者发现老板支持共和党，便在标题中突出“共和党支持者经营的餐馆发生中毒事件”。字面上也许句句属实，但读者会产生什么联想？

如果老板支持民主党，是否也要同样处理？如果不需要，原来的政治标签又有什么必要？

新闻选择本身就能影响读者判断。不必造假，也能产生偏向。

何况这起案件还有一个更加复杂的事实：枪手涉嫌杀害自己的家人。杀害父母和姐姐，与在旅游广场射杀陌生人，究竟有什么联系？是个人恩怨、政治狂热，还是其他原因？目前都需要调查。不能因为发现一个政治标签，就把所有疑问打包解决。

真正严肃的新闻，应当追究警方为何未能提前发现危险，枪手如何取得大量武器，是否存在被忽视的预警，以及死伤者能否获得应有的救助。

至于凶手左还是右，只有与犯罪动机存在经过证实的联系，才具有相应的解释价值。

现代政治已经够热闹了。有人把经济问题分左右，把教育问题分左右，连吃什么、开什么车都能分左右。如今有人杀了人，也急着把尸体搬上政治光谱，仿佛不贴上标签，死者便白死了。

杀人犯首先是杀人犯。法律应当根据行为和证据追究责任，而不是根据政治阵营决定罪恶的颜色。

一个社会如果连悼念无辜死者，都要先弄清凶手属于哪一派，恐怕最需要调查的，已经不只是凶手了。

关键词: 
杀人犯
波兰
栏目: 
新颖视角
首页重点发表: 
新鲜看点
作者: 
迟迟浙

item.title: 波兰悼念克拉科夫枪击案遇难者
item.description:
来源: 
博谈网

波兰11月8日开始为期两天的全国哀悼，悼念前一天发生在克拉科夫市中心大规模枪击事件中的遇难者。事件造成6人死亡、多人受伤，其中包括外国游客。

据路透社和美联社报道，一名24岁男子7日驾车闯入克拉科夫老城主广场，随后向人群开枪。警方赶到现场后与枪手交火，两名警员受伤，枪手也被击伤，目前仍在医院接受治疗。

遇难者包括4名女性和2名男性，其中一人为英国公民。伤者包括来自德国、奥地利、葡萄牙、俄罗斯和英国的游客。

警方随后在距离克拉科夫约150公里的一处住宅内发现枪手父母及姐姐的遗体，三人均有疑似枪伤。调查人员怀疑这些死亡事件与枪手有关，目前已查获11支枪械及大量弹药。

波兰检察机关已就谋杀、谋杀未遂及涉嫌恐怖主义犯罪展开调查，具体作案动机尚待查明。

克拉科夫老城部分街道继续封闭，民众在广场点燃蜡烛、献花悼念遇难者。波兰政府下令全国降半旗致哀，首都华沙等地也加强了公共场所的安全警戒。

 

关键词: 
波兰

item.title: U.S. forces are ready to strike Iran, but Trump doubts they'll need to
item.description:
President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it is “highly unlikely” he will need to order the US back to war with Iran as long as there is progress in negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, repeating his assertion five times during an interview with CNN.

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump told CNN’s Jim Sciutto during a 20-minute phone interview, referring to Iran. “The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”

“So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to,” he continued. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.”

‘We’re ready for it’

Eight months after the war started, the two sides have been in a stalemate, with little military action or significant diplomatic progress made while oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz have come under Iranian attack.

The two countries and officials from Qatar, which has mediated the talks, have kept quiet about the status of their negotiations. But Iranian hardliners have seized on the results of last week’s midterm elections — fueled in part by the war’s unpopularity with US voters — as a sign of a weakened Trump presidency that would be more willing to given in to their country’s demands to be allowed to continue its nuclear program, which it says it needs for energy, and maintain control of the strait.

Iran has also struggled to sell crude oil on global markets under US sanctions, while billions of dollars in assets held in foreign banks have been frozen.

Trump, who has in the past offered mixed messages about his willingness to end the war, made clear during the interview that US forces are in position in the region if he were to give the order to strike. “We’re ready for it. I’ve got three aircraft carriers here. The other one just arrived. We have three. They’re fully locked and loaded,” he said.

The president also said that the US has identified infrastructure targets inside Iran in the event of renewed military action, including power plants and bridges. “We have 38 bridges in our site that we can knock down in literally one hour, “ he said. “They’ll all be down.”

However, he said he would prefer not to destroy Iranian infrastructure. “I don’t want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them,” he said. “I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder.”

Diplomatic activity across the Middle East has increased since Tuesday’s midterm elections.

On Friday, Qatar said that Trump had called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss de-escalation, and a day earlier, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke with his counterparts from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Oman, Pakistan, Kuwait, Jordan, Turkey, Cyprus and Qatar.

Depleted Iranian stockpiles

In terms of Iran’s ability to defend against new US strikes, Trump said Iran’s air defenses have been destroyed. “It’s unstoppable because they have no anti-aircraft stuff. All of their anti-aircraft is gone,” he said.

The president also provided new details on the state of Iranian missile and drone stockpiles, saying that the regime maintains 10% of its missile capacity and 15% of its drone capabilities.

“The only thing they can do is about 10% level — make some missiles and make some drones. Drones at about 15% because much of their factories are gone,” he said.

“Most likely it will not be necessary,” he repeated about the prospect of new military action. “They want to make a deal so badly.”

CNN’s Mostafa Salem contributed to this story.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/08/politics/trump-interview-on-iran

item.title: 埃及两列火车相撞7死112伤
item.description:
来源: 
博谈网

埃及11月8日发生严重铁路事故，两列客运火车在首都开罗以南相撞，造成至少7人死亡、112人受伤。埃及当局已展开调查，伤亡人数较最初公布的数字明显上升。

据路透社和美联社报道，事故发生在吉萨省阿亚特地区，距离开罗约50多公里。一列从吉萨开往法尤姆的客运列车，追尾另一列从开罗开往阿斯旺的列车，导致部分车厢脱轨。现场画面显示，多节车厢倾斜或翻倒在铁轨附近，救援人员和当地居民参与搜救。

埃及卫生部门表示，事故造成7人死亡、112人受伤，死者包括一名列车司机。伤者已被送往附近医院接受治疗，有关部门派出救护车及救援设备处理事故。

埃及总统塞西要求立即查明事故原因，调查是否存在人为失误或安全管理问题，并依法追究相关责任。目前官方尚未公布事故的具体原因。

埃及铁路系统近年来多次发生重大事故，老旧设备、信号系统和安全管理问题长期受到关注。2002年，阿亚特地区曾发生严重列车火灾，造成数百人死亡。

关键词:

item.title: Immigration crackdown isn't expected to ease after GOP election losses
item.description:
The Trump administration is unlikely to scale back its aggressive crackdown on illegal immigration following the results of the midterm elections, multiple U.S. officials told CBS News, citing the elevation of immigration hawk Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Republicans suffered huge losses across the country on Election Day, including in some historically red states like Texas. Exit polls indicated that immigration was one of the top issues, alongside the economy, among Texas Latinos, who swung heavily toward Democrats. And 58% of voters nationwide said the Trump administration's deportation crackdown had "gone too far." 

In January, Democratic lawmakers will take control of both chambers of Congress and assume sweeping powers to investigate the administration's immigration crackdown and its most controversial policies.

Still, officials at the Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement have not received instructions to reduce immigration enforcement since the election, the sources said, requesting anonymity because they were not authorized to talk to the media.

In recent weeks, ICE officials have been instructed to try to carry out around 19,000 arrests per week, or about 2,700 per day, an increase from a prior 2,000 daily arrest target, agency sources told CBS News. That target was set before the midterms.

The U.S. officials cited Miller's appointment to the top post in the White House as a clear indication the Trump administration is likely to continue ICE's deportation blitz, as well as its quieter yet far-reaching campaign to sharply restrict legal immigration.

Asked if the midterms would usher in a pullback in immigration enforcement, one of the officials responded, "I would count on the opposite" with Miller as chief of staff.

The sources also said the administration believes the stunning electoral losses last week were largely driven by concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran — not its immigration crackdown.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorize our communities. There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News.

Bis cited the Trump administration's efforts to bolster security at the U.S.-Mexico border, where illegal crossings have plunged to historically low levels after soaring to record highs under former President Joe Biden's tenure.

In a statement Sunday, DHS said ICE would not be "backing away or slowing down."

"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets," DHS added.

Miller has been seen as a loyal foot soldier in Mr. Trump's inner circle for a decade, since his successful 2016 presidential campaign, when he promised to shut down Muslim immigration to the U.S. and dramatically expand deportations of those in the U.S. illegally.

During that time, Miller has solidified himself as the chief architect of Mr. Trump's hardline immigration policies. Miller was one of Mr. Trump's top aides during his first administration, when officials banned immigration and travel from Muslim-majority countries and separated thousands of migrant children from their parents as part of a "zero tolerance" crackdown that was abandoned after massive public uproar.

But Miller has greatly expanded his power — and his influence over federal immigration policymaking — since Mr. Trump's return to the White House. 

In less than two years, with Miller as deputy chief of staff and homeland security adviser, the second Trump administration has effectively closed the U.S. asylum system; shut down refugee admissions, with a notable exemption for White South Africans; tightened access to different legal immigration benefits like green cards; and undertaken highly visible ICE and Border Patrol arrest operations across the country. 

Those immigration enforcement operations have often triggered widespread community backlash, including in January, when federal immigration officials killed two American citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during a crackdown in Minneapolis that the administration scaled back following bipartisan outcry.

Miller has publicly floated the idea of suspending habeas corpus — the conditional right for people to challenge unlawful detention — for ICE detainees. Habeas cases have skyrocketed over the past two years, as the Trump administration has greatly narrowed other avenues for those fighting deportation to be released from ICE detention.

In addition to his immigration portfolio, Miller has also played an influential role in the Trump administration's crackdown on universities and legal groups, and its campaign to investigate allegations of fraud in Democratic-led states like Minnesota.

Theresa Cardinal Brown, an immigration official at DHS during the Obama and Bush administrations, said the Trump administration's deportation efforts are likely to face some obstacles next year. She expects congressional Democrats to use their new powers to try to rein in ICE, including by issuing a flurry of subpoenas, holding oversight hearings and passing measures to limit immigration enforcement funds.

Cardinal Brown also predicts that some communities and states with newly elected Democratic leaders, like Texas, may scrap or limit policies that allowed or required local law enforcement officials to work with ICE. Last week, Houston's mayor said he would direct local police to limit their cooperation with ICE, following the election results.

But Cardinal Brown stressed that Mr. Trump will likely veto any Democratic attempts to restrict ICE enforcement and noted the agency received $75 billion in funds through 2029 due to the "One Big Beautiful Bill" that the president signed into law last year.

"They're going to continue apace," Cardinal Brown said. "They have the money. They have the resources."

This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-crackdown-stephen-miller-illegal-immigration/

item.title: 马斯克看好太空算力前景
item.description:
来源: 
来稿

特斯拉及SpaceX首席执行官马斯克近日公开赞同谷歌联合创始人拉里·佩奇关于未来计算资源将大规模转向太空的预测。随着人工智能产业对算力和能源的需求不断增长，太空数据中心正成为科技企业探索的新方向。

马斯克11月8日在社交平台X转发一段有关佩奇预测的帖子，并表示，佩奇曾作出许多准确预测，这也是其中之一。

据投资播客《Invest Like the Best》主持人帕特里克·奥肖内西转述，佩奇曾预测，未来99.999%的计算资源最终将部署在太空。不过，这一数字并非经过科学验证的预测，也没有明确实现期限，主要表达了对太空计算长期前景的高度乐观。

马斯克此前也多次表示，随着太空发射成本下降及太阳能利用技术进步，将大型计算设施部署到轨道上，未来可能具备经济优势。

SpaceX已开始推动相关计划。今年1月，该公司向美国联邦通信委员会申请，计划建设由最多100万颗卫星组成的轨道数据中心网络。监管机构随后受理申请并征求公众意见，但这不代表计划已经获得最终批准。

按照设想，轨道计算设施可以直接利用太阳能发电，减少对地面电网、土地和水资源的依赖，并通过卫星通信网络传输数据。

推动这一设想的另一个现实背景，是美国地面数据中心建设面临日益复杂的审批和基础设施问题。

投资人马丁·卡萨多近日在播客访谈中指出，美国部分地区出现大量针对数据中心建设的限制性立法提案，企业正在考虑将更多计算设施部署到海外甚至太空，以降低对单一地区监管环境的依赖。

不过，太空数据中心仍面临一系列技术与经济挑战，包括卫星发射成本、轨道散热、辐射防护、设备寿命、维护更换及通信延迟等问题。太空拥有太阳能资源，但在真空环境下，计算设备产生的热量必须主要通过辐射方式排出。

国际能源署数据显示，全球数据中心用电量已达到每年数百太瓦时，人工智能发展预计将进一步推动需求增长。

目前，太空计算尚未形成能够与大型地面数据中心竞争的成熟商业体系。佩奇和马斯克的表态反映了科技界对这一方向的长期预期，而SpaceX提出的卫星网络计划，则是推动这一设想走向实际部署的初步行动。

item.title: Battle between Congress and Trump looms as he vows political comeback
item.description:
Donald Trump vowed a political comeback Sunday as the major parties clashed over Democrat threats to prosecute top administration officials after the president's Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections.

The devastating results in last Tuesday's vote leave Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the remaining two-year 'lame duck' period of his White House tenure, while opening the door to multiple investigations by the Democrat-controlled Congress of the president, his family and senior members of his administration.

On political talk shows Sunday, incoming congressional leaders from the Democratic Party promised to hold Trump and his aides to account, while the president's top law officer resolved to defend them and Trump dug in his heels on social media.

"America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election," Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the stock market that had grown during his tenure took a loss after the vote.

"But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!"

On Friday, a defiant Trump appointed hardline advisor Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback -- even though many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have reflected on why they had lost so badly at the ballot box.

Miller was architect of Trump's tough immigration policy that analysts have identified as a contributing factor to the unpopularity of Republicans.

Amid Democrat threats for administration officials to "lawyer up," Trump said Saturday he was ordering the Justice Department to examine Democratic threats to impeach members of his administration, likening it to "extortion."

- 'They can come after us' -

That stance stoked a war of words between top Republicans and Democrats on the Sunday talk shows.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump and now head of the Justice Department, vowed to actively defend Trump and senior members of his administration.

"You have members of Congress who, after Tuesday, have done nothing but threaten everything that's happening in this administration," Blanche told CNN, citing impeachment threats against Miller after his appointment.

"If they try to come after Stephen Miller...instead of actually just conducting oversight and leading, of course the Department of Justice will be there to defend him."

Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, took aim at Blanche, saying one role of Congress under the US constitution is to hold the executive branch to account.

"All he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump's cabinet and administration officials. That is not his job," Garcia told CNN, vowing to stop corruption and investigate "those that are committing crimes against the American public."

"They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated," added Garcia.

With control of committees in both chambers of Congress, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny.

Likely subjects include the Trump family's business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war.

Hakeem Jeffries, set to become speaker of the new Democrat-controlled House of Representatives, said he would support an effort to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of the war on Iran that began in February.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC, when asked about a Republican lawmaker's reported plan to introduce an impeachment motion as early as Monday.

"The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go."

During his first presidency, Trump himself was impeached by the House twice, but on both occasions he was acquitted by the Senate.

msp/md

This article originally appeared on AFP at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trump-vows-comeback-bitter-showdown-160116637.html

item.title: El-Sayed says he is 'happy' to work with Trump on Medicare for all and other priorities
item.description:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday opened the door to potentially working with President Donald Trump to pass legislation securing nationwide affordable healthcare.

In an interview with ABC’s “This Week,” the progressive from Michigan called Trump an “unserious fool” but said he would be “happy” to sit down with the president to discuss how best to serve Michiganders.

“Look, I've never met the man. I am — he is the president of the United States. I am the U.S. senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him like I'll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on: to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All,” El-Sayed said. “I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump Care for All, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game. Let's see if he wants to do that.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump was vociferous in his criticism of El-Sayed throughout the campaign season, lambasting El-Sayed for his progressive policies and repeatedly mocking his name.

Trump had supported former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the bitter Michigan race. El-Sayed on Sunday said he is not aware of any attempts at communication from Rogers.

"I think he has a flight to catch to Florida," El-Sayed quipped. Though born and raised in Michigan, Rogers moved to Florida with his wife after leaving Congress in 2015. (Rogers' campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

Despite his apparent openness to meet with Trump, El-Sayed criticized the president for appointing Stephen Miller to be the White House’s new chief of staff — evidence, El-Sayed argued, of Trump’s lack of seriousness when Americans are demanding affordability and accountability.

“So, look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," he said. "He is the president of the United States, but he wants to continue to fool he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House. And he gets to choose where he goes next."

This article originally appeared on Politico at https://www.politico.com/news/2026/11/08/el-sayed-work-with-trump-medicare-01155555

item.title: Stephen Miller and the DOJ reportedly plan to throw journalists in jail over leaks
item.description:
Newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and the Department of Justice have reportedly been considering throwing journalists in jail to get them to reveal their sources when government intel is leaked, according to a report.

Following Susie Wiles’ exit as chief of staff, The Atlantic reported that President Donald Trump urged the DOJ to pursue criminal-leak investigations on national security grounds.

There have reportedly been discussions among White House officials about tactics they could use to get journalists to reveal their sources — including arresting them, three people familiar with the subject told the outlet.

Two people described Wiles pushing back against trying to force journalists to divulge their government sources, while Miller was in favor of the move, insisting that it wouldn’t take long for journalists to give up their sources, according to the report.

A DOJ spokesperson told The Atlantic: “This is absolutely false,” and reiterated that when approached for comment by The Independent.

Meanwhile, a White House spokesperson told The Independent: “Unauthorized leaks of sensitive national security information will NEVER be tolerated. They endanger American lives and threaten our national security. Those responsible must be held accountable.”

It is not illegal for journalists to receive — and write about — classified information they have received from a government leaker, even if the source themselves has violated the law by sharing the information.

In 1971, The New York Times published excerpts of a leaked report detailing the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War, prompting the Nixon administration to try and block the publication of the leaked files. However, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the newspaper and press freedom.

On Friday, Trump revealed that his longtime aide, Miller, would be replacing Wiles, who Trump was reportedly “furious” with after Republicans lost control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a time when the Republican Party's midterm defeat could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

Miller, 41, is one of Trump’s longest-serving aides and one of only a few who have worked for the president throughout both his first and second terms in office.

However, he is best known for driving Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown, which has been widely unpopular among Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of Trump’s mass deportation agenda, with 54% disapproving.

Still, Trump announced Miller as Wiles’ replacement on Friday.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” he wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

This article originally appeared on The Independent at https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/americas/us-politics/stephen-miller-doj-journalists-jail-report-b3081234.html
